claims.claim: Kullmann inverts Lubbock/Friedman: the omniscient archaic passages are the vivid visual 'showing', while point-of-view passages mainly serve to show states of mind rather than to describe action (p. 120).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: mainly serve to show certain states of mind

claims.claim: Kullmann notes the shift from Genette's focalisation externe to focalisation interne on Frodo, who becomes Bal's 'focalisé' or Lanser's 'focalizer', but he prefers the historical term 'point of view' (p. 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: hobbit viewpoint vs archaic speech registers
claims.claim: The archaic register of Dwarves and Men contrasts starkly with the language of the hobbits and of the narrator, who usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view (p. 217).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view

claims.claim: Turner: Kullmann's psychonarration, events filtered through an individual's limited point of view, is typical of the realistic novel; where no hobbits are present the focus on 'archaic' characters brings narrative language of an older epic tradition.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Turner: K&S dispel any notion of one 'Tolkien style', showing skilful use of several styles resonating with the last few hundred years of English writing.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)
claims.quote: dispel any notion that there is any one ‘Tolkien style’

claims.feature: parataxis vs hypotaxis as cultural registers
claims.claim: Bolding reports Kullmann's contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis as defining the Rohirrim and Gondor cultures, with Gandalf the one speaker who moves fluidly between social registers.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: his contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis

claims.claim: Bolding summarises ch. 9: Gandalf and Frodo are the most flexible speakers, Sam undergoes the most evolution, Gimli and Legolas keep the most traditional registers, Merry and Pippin use common English as reality-based touchstones.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: Gandalf and Frodo are found to be the most flexible

claims.claim: Holmes cites K&S data that Aragorn opens future pronouncements with 'shall' half again as often as Gandalf and seven times as often as Sam or Pippin.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: seven times as often as Sam or Pippin

claims.claim: Holmes: K&S's data tend to refute the long-held view of the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions in Tolkien (K&S p. 40).
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions

claims.claim: Holmes: Kullmann identifies 45 to 50 intercalated stories told by twenty-three characters, in three categories (simultaneous events, exposition, mythological past); Bolding gives 23 storytellers.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: 45 to 50 “intercalated” stories told by twenty-three characters

claims.claim: Siepmann's syntax chapter uses a corpus separating dialogue from narrative, with the PHRASEOROM post-war fiction corpus and the BNC as references, extracting the most significant 3- to 6-grams of syntactic tags and attending to constructions Tolkien avoids as well as prefers.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings' (ch. 3) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: constructions that Tolkien, compared to other authors, tends to avoid

claims.claim: Siepmann finds that the short copular sentences and modal 'would' uses that signal free indirect speech in modern fiction are conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings (pp. 75-76).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings

claims.feature: inner monologue rendered by omniscient narrator
claims.claim: Short sentences of the kind found in modern fiction tend to be direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue, a strategy Tolkien does not use (p. 75).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue

claims.claim: Instead of free indirect thought Tolkien overuses clauses reporting a character's thoughts with a that-clause ('He thought that he had heard a faint voice') and 'It seemed that' constructions (p. 84).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: It seemed that he had made some decision

claims.claim: At clause level the first thing to note is an evident underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position, against the contemporary-fiction patterns 'She longed to say it', 'He had expected to fight' (p. 74).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position

verdicts.trueWording: p.120: "passages which feature a particular point of view mainly serve to show certain states of mind, rather than illustrating a story"; just before it, "[the passages about the Riders of] Rohan quoted above, could certainly be described as extremely vivid. Usually, they are about visual impressions, so that 'showing' might actually be an adequate term"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume 9uAsEAAAQBAJ (jscmd=SearchWithinVolume JSON, verbatim book text with page numbers); the volume landing page itself carries no preview text. Quote 'mainly serve to show certain states of mind' is word for word on p.120. Every limb checked by stitching overlapping snippets of the same page: p.120 sets up Lubbock and Friedman 'following Henry James, set particular store by the opposition between telling and showing, with telling being the province of an omniscient narrator, and showing occurring in passages in which a particular point of view is expressed'; the Rohan (omniscient, archaic-register) passages are then called 'extremely vivid ... about visual impressions, so that "showing" might actually be an adequate term'; and p.121 makes the inversion explicit - 'the opposite is the case: if we apply the terms of diegesis and mimesis to the Tolkien passages discussed, the Riders of Rohan passages may strike us as mimetic rather than diegetic'. Only wording difference: the book says point-of-view passages show states of mind 'rather than illustrating a story', which the claim renders 'rather than to describe action' - same import.

verdicts.trueWording: p.123: "'focalisation externe' (the narrator focusing his attention on Frodo) to 'focalisation interne' (the narration records Frodo's point of view); Frodo becomes the 'focalise' (Bal 38) or 'focalizer' (Lanser 141-143)"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume. Quote 'Frodo becomes the "focalise"' is word for word on p.123, with the externe-to-interne shift and both attributions (Bal 38 / Lanser 141-143) in the same sentence. The preference limb is supported one page earlier, in the note apparatus at p.122: the traditional point-of-view terminology '(Lubbock, Friedman), in preference to the more sophisticated terminology which revolves around the concept of "focalization", cf. Genette 194-200; Bal 21-58; Lanser 140-148; Nunning'. Two small wording points, neither an unsupported limb: the book's word is 'traditional' rather than the claim's 'historical' (though note 9 on p.123 does call for 'a historical investigation of this phenomenon'), and that preference sentence sits on p.122, not the cited p.123. Genette is the attributed source of the focalization terminology at p.122n5 rather than beside the two French terms themselves.

verdicts.trueWording: p.217: "The archaic register used by Dwarves and Men forms a stark contrast to the language of the hobbits and of the narrator, who, as we have seen, usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume. The quote 'usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view' is word for word on p.217, and the whole claim sentence is a near-transcription of the book's sentence on that page - archaic register, Dwarves and Men, stark contrast, hobbits and narrator, all present. Page number confirmed as 217 by the search-inside page id. p.216 corroborates the register point: 'Dwarves and Men, rather speak in ways which do not encourage interruption. We may call their ways of speaking "literary"...'.

verdicts.trueWording: "This psychonarration ... is typical of the realistic novel"
verdicts.note: Route: live euppublishing.com returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and a browser-user-agent curl; recovered from the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20220615121435id_/https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/full/10.3366/ink.2022.0144, which carries Turner's full open-access review text. Graded SUBSTANCE rather than VERBATIM only because the claim carries no quote field to match; the review's own sentences are all but identical: 'This psychonarration, in which events are filtered through the limited point of view of an individual, is typical of the realistic novel. However, in the episodes in which no hobbits are present to act as mediators, the focus on the more "archaic" characters is reflected in narrative language more typical of an older, epic tradition which constitutes a contrasting set of pre-texts.' Both limbs supported, and the review attributes the chapter to Kullmann ('Chapter 4 concentrates on focalisation. For most of the story, Kullmann argues...').

verdicts.trueWording: "Certainly they dispel any notion that there is any one 'Tolkien style' ... they demonstrate that he made skilful use of a number of different styles which resonate with a broad cross-section of the last few hundred years of writing in English"
verdicts.note: Route: Wayback raw capture of the EUP page (live host 403s). Quote 'dispel any notion that there is any one "Tolkien style"' is word for word. Second limb also verbatim in the following sentence - 'skilful use of a number of different styles which resonate with a broad cross-section of the last few hundred years of writing in English'.

verdicts.trueWording: "his contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis as defining these two cultures on scales of sophistication"; "The one person who fluidly moves between societies, languages, and social registers is Gandalf"
verdicts.note: Route: dc.swosu.edu landing page fetched live, but its viewcontent.cgi PDF 403s to curl even with a browser user agent and referer; recovered from the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20230512052131id_/https://dc.swosu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3118&context=mythlore and text-extracted from the PDF. Quote is word for word. 'These two cultures' resolves in the preceding sentence to 'military communities such as the Riders of Rohan and the defenders of Minas Tirith', i.e. the claim's Rohirrim and Gondor - a paraphrase of the review's own naming, not an unsupported limb. Gandalf limb is verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: "Gandalf and Frodo are found to be the most flexible. Sam undergoes the most evolution. Gimli and Legolas represent the most traditional registers for their typology. Merry and Pippen use common English language as befitting their role of reality-based touchstones"
verdicts.note: Route: Wayback raw PDF capture of the Mythlore review (live PDF 403s). All four speaker limbs are verbatim in four consecutive sentences; the quote matches word for word. Two notes, neither an unsupported limb: Bolding identifies the chapter as 'The penultimate chapter "Language and Character"' rather than by number, and Holmes's review (this chunk's other source, scholar.valpo.edu vol14/iss1/7) independently pins that chapter as 'Chapter 9 ("Language and Character", both authors)'; and the review prints the character name as 'Pippen', a typo the claim silently corrects to 'Pippin'.

verdicts.trueWording: "why Aragorn begins a pronouncement about the future with shall half again as often as Gandalf does, and seven times as often as Sam or Pippin"
verdicts.note: Route: scholar.valpo.edu landing page fetched live; its viewcontent.cgi PDF 403s to curl, recovered from the Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250602182646id_/https://scholar.valpo.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1257&context=journaloftolkienresearch and text-extracted. Quote 'seven times as often as Sam or Pippin' is word for word, and both ratio limbs plus 'begins a pronouncement about the future with shall' are in the same sentence. Holmes presents it as one of K&S's findings ('those findings that will be ... useful to some future writer on Tolkien who wonders why...').

verdicts.trueWording: "Other results tend to refute long-held views (like the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions; see K & S p. 40)"
verdicts.note: Route: Wayback raw PDF capture of the Journal of Tolkien Research review (live PDF 403s). verdicts.trueWording: Holmes: "Chapter 7 ('Storytelling,' Kullmann) identifies three categories of the 45 to 50 'intercalated' stories told by twenty-three characters in the novel: simultaneous events, exposition, and 'mythological' past"; Bolding: "there are 23 story tellers"
verdicts.note: Route: Wayback raw PDF captures of both reviews. The quote '45 to 50 "intercalated" stories told by twenty-three characters' is word for word in Holmes, along with the Kullmann attribution and all three category names. The final limb is attributed in the claim itself to Bolding, and it checks out on the Mythlore review (also fetched for 663/664): 'while there are 23 story tellers, each with their own style, the common purpose is to give historic context to the quest'.

verdicts.trueWording: Springer abstract: "Drawing on a corpus which separates dialogue and narrative sections ... Using the imaginative prose section of the PHRASEOROM corpus (post-war fiction) and the British National Corpus as a reference, we extracted the statistically most significant 3-grams, 4-grams, 5-grams and 6-grams. The chapter pays equal attention to constructions that Tolkien, compared to other authors, tends to avoid, and to those that he prefers"
verdicts.note: link.springer.com itself is unreachable: the live chapter URL, the doi.org redirect and springerprofessional.de all serve the same 3,038-byte JavaScript 'Client Challenge' page; the Wayback CDX index holds no capture of the chapter page (only a 2021 capture of the book page, which carries no chapter abstracts) and Save Page Now returned 520; the chapter is closed access (Unpaywall oa_status 'closed', no OA locations) so there is no PDF to extract; and Crossref, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all return a null abstract (Semantic Scholar explicitly says the abstract field was 'elided by the publisher'). Recovered instead through a publisher-abstract mirror of the DOI, https://colab.ws/articles/10.1007%2F978-3-030-69299-5_3, which carries the complete abstract verbatim rather than a summary or a snippet - the quote 'constructions that Tolkien, compared to other authors, tends to avoid' is word for word there, as are the dialogue/narrative corpus split, PHRASEOROM post-war fiction, the BNC as reference, and the most significant 3- to 6-grams of syntactic tags. Independently corroborated in the book's own chapter 3 body text via Google Books search-inside: p.72 'PHRASEOROM corpus (post-war fiction) and the British National Corpus as a reference. We were as interested in the kinds of constructions that Tolkien, com-pared to other authors, tends to avoid, as in those that he prefers', and p.70/71 'most significant 3-grams, 4-grams, 5-grams and 6-grams (i.e. sequences of syntactic tags of the type N + ADJ)'. The 'Siepmann's chapter' attribution is supported by the running foot 'D. Siepmann' on the chapter's pages and by Holmes's review ('Chapter 3 ("Narrative Syntax," Siepmann)'); the Springer listing itself credits both authors.

verdicts.trueWording: pp.75-76: "This may be due to the fact that Tolkien does not use free indirect speech, since short sentences like these tend to be direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue. By the same token, then, uses of the modal would which indicate free indirect speech are conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume; the sentence straddles the page break and was reconstructed from overlapping snippets returned for p.75 and p.76, matching the claim's cited span pp.75-76. Quote 'conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings' is word for word on p.76. Both limbs hold: the short copular sentences are the immediately preceding item ('copular be and a subject complement. Merely a hollow formality. / She was not an optimistic woman. / Not the usual sort. / Hardly a submissive voice!'), presented in section 3.2 - which p.72 identifies as the section that 'deals with dispreferred constructions' - and the 'by the same token' carries the absence over to the modal-would uses. Strictly, the words 'conspicuous by their absence' are attached in the text to the would-uses, and the copular sentences' absence is stated in the surrounding dispreferred-constructions framing.

verdicts.trueWording: p.75: "Tolkien does not use free indirect speech, since short sentences like these tend to be direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume; snippet page id confirms p.75, matching the claim's citation. Quote 'direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue' is word for word. 'Short sentences of the kind found in modern fiction' matches the book's 'short sentences like these', where 'these' are the contemporary-fiction examples listed immediately before ('Merely a hollow formality. / She was not an optimistic woman. / Not the usual sort. / Hardly a submissive voice!'). 'A strategy Tolkien does not use' matches the page's 'Tolkien does not use free indirect speech' - the book names the strategy free indirect speech and equates it in the same sentence with these direct renditions of inner monologue.

verdicts.trueWording: p.84: "[a] that-clause reporting a character's thoughts. He knew that it had become aware of his gaze. He thought that he had heard a faint voice answering him ... A variant of this involves the use of seem: It seemed that they had vanished from the North. It seemed that he had made some decision"
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume; all snippets return page id 84, matching the citation. Quote 'It seemed that he had made some decision' is word for word, as is the claim's parenthetical example 'He thought that he had heard a faint voice' (the book continues '...answering him'). The that-clause construction and the 'It seemed that' variant are both on p.84, and the passage sits in the chapter's overused/preferred-constructions run (the next sentence begins 'Another common novelistic motif that is overrepresented in The Lord of the Rings...'). One terminology point, not an unsupported limb: the book nowhere uses the phrase 'free indirect thought' (zero search-inside hits); its term is free indirect speech, and the 'instead of' relation is established at pp.75-76, where the absence of free indirect speech is stated.

verdicts.trueWording: p.74: "the first thing to note is an evident underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position. Typical sentence patterns found in contemporary fiction are the following: She longed to say it / He had expected to fight / It must have cost her ..."
verdicts.note: Route: Google Books search-inside on the cited volume; snippet page id confirms p.74, matching the citation, and the page's running foot reads '74 D. The quoted phrase appears as 'an evident unde-ruse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position' - the hyphen is a line-break artifact of the scanned page, so the phrase-search for the unbroken string returns zero and the match had to be made through the neighbouring phrase 'the first thing to note'; on the page itself it is word for word.
